name: Pharmacology - antidotes & mechanisms
description: Classic antidotes, drug mechanisms and monitoring parameters. Study aid only - not clinical guidance.

cards.question: Antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose?
cards.answer: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) - replenishes glutathione so NAPQI can be detoxified. Most effective within 8 hours of ingestion.

cards.question: Antidote for warfarin over-anticoagulation?
cards.answer: Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione). Add 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (or FFP if unavailable) when there is major bleeding.

cards.question: Antidote for opioid overdose?
cards.answer: Naloxone - a competitive opioid receptor antagonist. Short half-life, so re-dosing or an infusion may be needed.

cards.question: Antidote for benzodiazepine overdose, and its main caveat?
cards.answer: Flumazenil. Caveat: it can precipitate seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users or mixed overdose (e.g. with TCAs), so it is rarely used.

cards.question: Antidote for unfractionated heparin?
cards.answer: Protamine sulfate. It only partially reverses low molecular weight heparin (roughly 60%).

cards.question: Antidote for organophosphate poisoning?
cards.answer: Atropine (blocks muscarinic effects) plus pralidoxime (reactivates acetylcholinesterase before ageing).

cards.question: Antidote for digoxin toxicity?
cards.answer: Digoxin-specific antibody Fab fragments (DigiFab). Also correct hyperkalaemia - but avoid calcium in classic teaching.

cards.question: Antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning?
cards.answer: Fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor); ethanol is the alternative. Haemodialysis for severe acidosis or high levels.

cards.question: Antidote for iron overdose?
cards.answer: Deferoxamine - a chelating agent given IV.

cards.question: First-line antidote for beta-blocker overdose?
cards.answer: Glucagon - raises cAMP independently of beta receptors. High-dose insulin/euglycaemia therapy is used in refractory cases.

cards.question: Mechanism of action of aspirin?
cards.answer: Irreversible acetylation of COX-1 and COX-2. At low dose it blocks platelet thromboxane A2 for the platelet's whole lifespan (~7-10 days).

cards.question: Mechanism of action of metformin?
cards.answer: Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases peripheral insulin sensitivity, largely via AMPK activation. Does not cause hypoglycaemia on its own.

cards.question: Mechanism and two classic side effects of ACE inhibitors?
cards.answer: Block angiotensin-converting enzyme, lowering angiotensin II and aldosterone. Classic side effects: dry cough (bradykinin) and hyperkalaemia; rarely angio-oedema.

cards.question: Mechanism of action of statins?
cards.answer: Competitive inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis, which up-regulates LDL receptors.

cards.question: Mechanism of action of proton pump inhibitors?
cards.answer: Irreversible inhibition of the gastric H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) in parietal cells.

cards.question: Which drug class do generic names ending in '-olol' belong to?
cards.answer: Beta-adrenergic receptor blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol).

cards.question: Two hallmark toxicities of aminoglycosides?
cards.answer: Nephrotoxicity (usually reversible) and ototoxicity (often irreversible). They also potentiate neuromuscular blockade.

cards.question: Which lab test monitors warfarin, and which monitors unfractionated heparin?
cards.answer: Warfarin: INR (derived from prothrombin time). Unfractionated heparin: aPTT (or anti-Xa).

cards.question: Which drugs classically cause gingival hyperplasia?
cards.answer: Phenytoin, ciclosporin and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine.

cards.question: The clinical triad of serotonin syndrome?
cards.answer: Altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (fever, tachycardia, sweating) and neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia - worse in the legs).

cards.question: Which antibiotic class is avoided in pregnancy and in young children because it stains teeth?
cards.answer: Tetracyclines - they bind calcium in developing teeth and bone.

cards.question: Why must beta-blockers be used cautiously with verapamil or diltiazem?
cards.answer: Additive negative chronotropic and inotropic effects - risk of severe bradycardia, AV block and heart failure.
